title: Removing Faults
note: This means a ruler keeping six faults out of himself: desire, anger, miserliness, false honour, excess joy and arrogance. Only those with understanding can see and remove them, so it follows that chapter.

couplets.plain: Those without pride, anger or pettiness have a prosperity with greatness in it.
couplets.pm: The wealth of rulers free of these three faults, drunkenness with wealth, anger and desire, has the nature of eminence. Desire beyond measure is called pettiness because it is the way of petty people. These faults lead to unjust acts, so the wealth of those who remove them goes the good way, lasts and is respected.
couplets.note: சிறுமை is literally smallness. He reads it as desire beyond measure.

links.reason: Pride is the first of three faults whose absence gives prosperity its greatness.
Named second of the three that must be gone for prosperity to have greatness.

links.remove: The Tamil says pettiness. Lust comes only from the old note and his gloss.

links.quote: a prosperity with greatness in it

couplets.plain: Miserliness, honour that has lost its nobility, and joy with no measure are faults in a ruler.
couplets.pm: Not giving where you should, honour that has parted from what is good, and joy beyond measure are faults in a ruler. Such honour means not bowing to sages, the worthy, great ascetics, elders, father and mother, and forcing through what you set out to do even when it can’t be done. Joy beyond measure means excessive favour to others.

links.reason: First of the ruler’s three faults, the hand that will not open.
His third fault is joy with no measure, being too pleased with how things stand.

links.quote: honour that has lost its nobility
links.reason: Honour that has lost its nobility is really pride, and it stands second of the three.

couplets.plain: Those who fear blame treat even a fault the size of a millet seed as if it were as big as a palmyra tree.
couplets.pm: If a fault the size of a millet seed arises in those who fear blame, they take it to be the size of a palmyra. It doesn’t suit them, so they won’t excuse it as small. They take it as great, grieve over it and guard against its coming again.

links.quote: as if it were as big as a palmyra tree
the size of a millet seed
links.reason: A millet seed grows into a palmyra tree in the eyes of those who fear blame.

couplets.plain: Guard against fault as your one aim. Fault is the enemy that brings your end.
couplets.pm: The enemy that brings your end is fault, so guard against it, making its absence your aim. As Sanskrit writers hold, enemies can bring no ruin except through these faults, so these are the real enemies. Having none of them is the same as having every good quality.

links.quote: Guard against fault as your one aim
links.reason: Makes guarding against your own faults the first charge, since they are the real enemy.

couplets.plain: Someone who doesn’t guard in advance will see their life perish, like a stack of straw before a fire.
couplets.pm: A ruler who doesn’t guard against a fault in the time before it comes will see his life destroyed when it comes, like a stack of straw facing a fire. However small the fault, great wealth is wholly ruined by it, as the simile shows.

links.reason: Shows the cost of not guarding in advance: sudden and total ruin.

links.quote: a stack of straw before a fire
links.reason: Someone unguarded is a stack of straw before a fire.

couplets.plain: If a ruler removes his own faults first, and then looks at those of others, what fault can he have?
couplets.pm: If a ruler first sees and removes his own faults and can then see the faults of others, what fault is left to him? Punishing others’ faults with his own uncorrected is itself a fault. With his own removed, it is justice. So only a ruler who has removed his own faults is fit to give justice.

links.quote: removes his own faults first, and then looks at those of others
If a ruler removes his own faults first
links.reason: Frames this as the safeguard of a ruler, who then has no fault left.

couplets.plain: The wealth of a miser who leaves undone what should be done won’t stay. It will perish.
couplets.pm: The wealth of someone who clings to it and doesn’t do what should be done with it perishes for nothing, with no chance of staying. What should be done is righteousness, more wealth and pleasure. Without righteousness and growth it can’t stay, and without pleasure from it, it simply perishes.

links.reason: Turns thrift against itself: wealth kept from what should be done with it perishes.

couplets.plain: The miserliness called a clinging heart is not to be counted with anything else.
couplets.pm: The clinging heart that won’t let wealth go where it should is not to be counted among other faults. It is worse than them all. Its nature is that, even where every good quality is present, it can push them down and rise above them. Other faults can’t do that.

links.quote: is not to be counted with anything else
links.reason: Refuses even to count it with anything else, as a thing apart.

couplets.plain: Never admire yourself. Don’t set your heart on deeds that bring no good.
couplets.pm: Even when you rise very high, don’t in your arrogance think highly of yourself, and don’t out of pride want deeds that bring you no good. Self-admiration keeps you from seeing place, time and strength, and makes you scorn righteousness and wealth. Deeds pursued only to finish what you set out to do bring sin, blame and ruin.

links.reason: Forbids admiring yourself at any time.

couplets.plain: If you can enjoy what you love without letting your love be known, the schemes of your enemies are useless.
couplets.pm: If you can enjoy the things you love without enemies knowing of your love, their plans to deceive you come to nothing. If they know, they enter by that door and deceive you. Desire, anger and joy aren’t to be wiped out entirely, so this shows how to enjoy desire, the chief of them. The others fall under the general ban.

links.quote: without letting your love be known
links.reason: Makes a hidden love the defence that leaves an enemy’s schemes with nothing to work on.
